turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How many push-ups should a beginner aim for?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Start with however many you can do with good form, even if it's five. Do three sets and try to add one rep each week.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if I can't do a single one?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then start with push-ups against a wall or a kitchen counter. As those get easy, move lower, to a chair and then the floor.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Knee push-ups count too, right?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Absolutely. They build the same muscles and they're a great step towards full push-ups.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Cool. And how often should I / do them, every day?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Every other day is better at first. Your muscles grow during the rest days.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I sit at a desk all day and my back is killing me. Are there exercises that help?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes. Bridges, bird dogs and gentle cat cow stretches strengthen and loosen your back. A few minutes a day helps.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What's a bird dog?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: On your hands and knees, you stretch one arm forward and the opposite leg back, hold for a few seconds, then switch.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sounds doable. Should I also get a standing desk or / is that overrated?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It can help, but mostly by making you change position. Getting up and walking around every half hour matters more.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Alright, I'll set a reminder on my phone.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good plan. And if the pain is sharp or doesn't improve, it's worth seeing a doctor.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it better to stretch before or after a run?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Before a run, do a dynamic warm-up like leg swings and easy jogging. Save the longer, held stretches for after.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why not hold stretches before?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Long static stretches can make your muscles feel a bit weaker right away. Moving warm-ups get them ready instead.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Makes sense. I usually just / start running and hope for the best.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lots of people do. Even five minutes of brisk walking first makes a real difference.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. And after, how long should I hold each stretch?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: About thirty seconds each. Focus on calves, hamstrings and hips, those get tight from running.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm sixty-eight and my doctor said I should do more exercise. I'm not really a gym person.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You don't need a gym. Brisk walking, swimming or a gentle yoga class are all excellent choices.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I do like swimming. How often should I go?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Two or three times a week is a great target. Start with twenty minutes and build up as you feel comfortable.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about strength? My doctor mentioned that too.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Simple things help a lot, like standing up from a chair without using your hands, or light weights at home.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I have some old dumbbells / somewhere in the garage, I think.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect. Try a few slow bicep curls and shoulder raises while watching television.

turns.text: Ha, that I can manage.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I tried running today and I was gasping after one minute. Is something wrong with me?

turns.text: Not at all, that's really normal when you're starting out. Most beginners go too fast.

turns.text: I wasn't even going fast. I don't think.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try slowing down until you could hold a conversation. It'll feel almost silly slow.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if I still can't last?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Mix running and walking. Run one minute, walk two, and repeat that six or seven times.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That sounds doable. How often / should I go out?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Three times a week, with a rest day in between. Each week, run a little longer and walk a little less.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I did my first leg day yesterday and now I can't walk down the stairs. Did I injure myself?

turns.text: Probably not. It sounds like normal muscle soreness, which usually peaks one or two days after a new workout.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It hurts so much. Sitting on the toilet is an event.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's very common after squats and lunges. It should ease in a few days.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I rest or move?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Gentle movement helps, like walking or easy cycling. Avoid another hard leg session until it fades.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Will it be this bad / every single time?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: No, your body adapts quickly. The next few leg days will feel much better, as long as you stay consistent.

turns.text: My goal this year is one single pull-up. I can't do even half of one.

turns.text: Great goal. Start with dead hangs, just hanging from the bar for as long as you can.

turns.text: Just hanging? That's it?

turns.text: It builds grip and shoulder strength. Then add negatives, jump up to the top and lower yourself as slowly as you can.

turns.text: How slow?

turns.text: Aim for three to five seconds on the way down. Do a few sets, two or three times a week.

turns.text: And rows, right? My trainer said something about rows / but I forgot.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, rows build the same back muscles. Inverted rows under a table or a bar are a good start.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. One pull-up by summer.

turns.text: Very realistic with that plan.

turns.text: Not stupid, but you have to be careful. Run early in the morning or late in the evening when it's cooler.

turns.text: Drink before you go and take some with you if you're out longer than half an hour. Wear light, loose clothing.

turns.text: How do I know if I'm / overdoing it?

turns.text: Dizziness, a headache, feeling sick or stopping sweating are warning signs. Stop, find shade and cool down right away.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Got it. Early mornings then.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Slow down a little too. Heat makes every pace feel harder.

turns.text: Is ten thousand steps a day actually a thing, or just a number someone made up?

turns.text: It's a bit of both. It started partly as a marketing number, but research does show more steps help your health.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So do I need ten thousand?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not exactly. Benefits seem to rise up to around seven or eight thousand for many people, and more is still good.

turns.text: I'm at like three thousand on a desk day.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then any increase is a win. Try a ten minute walk after each meal.

turns.text: After every meal? / That's a lot.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Even after lunch alone gets you over a thousand extra steps. Start there and add more if you like it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My lower back hurts when I hold a plank. Am I doing it wrong?

turns.text: Probably your hips are sagging. Try squeezing your glutes and pulling your belly button in slightly.

turns.text: My glutes? For a plank?

turns.text: Good for him, but it's not a competition. Build up slowly, and if your back still hurts, try planks on your knees first.

turns.text: Something you can control for fifteen swings with good form. For many people, that's eight to twelve kilos.

turns.text: Perfect starting point. Practice in a clear space, away from that window.

turns.text: How do I get rid of belly fat? I do a hundred sit-ups every night.

turns.text: Unfortunately sit-ups won't burn fat from your belly specifically. You can't really target fat loss in one spot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Then what's the point of them?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: They strengthen your core, which is good. But losing belly fat comes from overall fat loss, through diet, activity and sleep.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So I should stop?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: No need to stop, but your time might be better spent on full body strength training and more walking.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And food-wise? I eat pretty healthy / mostly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Small steady changes work best, like more protein and vegetables, fewer sugary drinks. Aim for slow progress, not a crash diet.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do I really need to warm up before lifting? It feels like a waste of time.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A short one is worth it. Five to ten minutes gets blood flowing and makes your first sets feel better.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What counts as a warm up?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A few minutes of light cardio, then some lighter sets of the lift you're about to do.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Lighter sets. Like how light?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: For example, if your working weight on squats is sixty kilos, do a set with the empty bar, then forty, then fifty.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's actually not that long. I always just / jump straight to my working weight.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's when people tweak something. A few warm up sets is cheap insurance.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I travel for work every week. How do I keep fit in hotel rooms?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Bodyweight circuits are perfect. Squats, push-ups, lunges, planks and burpees need no equipment at all.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Burpees. I hate burpees.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Everybody does. You can swap them for fast mountain climbers.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long should a circuit take?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Twenty minutes is plenty. Do each exercise for forty seconds with twenty seconds rest, and repeat the round four times.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's quiet enough / for a thin wall hotel?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Mostly, yes. Skip jumping moves late at night if you're worried about the neighbors.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Smart. Resistance bands too?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, they weigh nothing and add a lot. Throw a pair in your suitcase.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My shins hurt every time I run. A sharp ache along the front.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That sounds like it could be shin splints, which is common when people increase their running too quickly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I did go from twice a week to five times.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's probably it. Cut back for a while and let them settle.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ice? Rest? I've heard both.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Both help. Ice for fifteen minutes after activity, and rest from running for a week or two. Swimming or cycling keep you fit meanwhile.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do my shoes / have anything to do with it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: They can. If they're worn out, replace them. And if the pain doesn't improve after a couple of weeks, see a doctor or physio.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Everyone at my gym takes creatine. Is it just hype?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's actually one of the most studied supplements. It helps with short, intense efforts like lifting and sprints.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it safe? My mum thinks it's like steroids.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's not a steroid. For healthy adults, research suggests it's safe at normal doses. Check with a doctor if you have kidney problems.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What's a normal dose?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Around three to five grams a day, every day. You don't need a loading phase.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Does it make you / like, puffy?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You may gain a little water weight in your muscles at first. That's normal and not fat.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, I'll tell my mum.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Maybe show her the research too. That usually helps.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My watch keeps talking about zone two training. What even is that?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's easy, steady exercise at a low heart rate, where you can still talk in full sentences.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That sounds too easy to do anything.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It builds your aerobic base, so your heart and muscles get better at using oxygen. Lots of endurance athletes spend most of their time there.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long do I have to do it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sessions of thirty to sixty minutes, a few times a week, tend to work well.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So I should slow down my runs? / My ego hates that.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most of them, yes. Keep one harder session a week for speed. Your ego will recover when you get faster.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I use a wheelchair and I want to build upper body strength. Where should I start?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Great goal. Resistance bands are a flexible place to start, you can anchor them to a door or your chair.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What exercises, though?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Seated rows, chest presses, shoulder presses and bicep curls all work well from your chair.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've also got a pair of dumbbells somewhere.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect. Add them for curls, overhead presses and lateral raises. Start light and focus on control.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My shoulders already / work hard pushing all day.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's an important point. Balance pushing with lots of pulling, like rows, to protect your shoulders. A physio with wheelchair experience could tailor a plan.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My father is seventy-nine and he had a fall last month. Are there exercises for balance?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, and they really help. Start with simple ones, like standing on one foot while holding a sturdy chair.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Holding a chair? He'd hate that.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Safety first, especially after a fall. As he gets steadier, he can hold on with just one finger.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What else?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Heel to toe walking along a hallway, and sit to stand from a chair without using his hands. Both build strength and balance.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: He's quite stubborn. He thinks exercise / is for young people.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Maybe frame it as staying independent rather than exercising. A tai chi class for seniors is also excellent for balance.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Tai chi might actually work. He likes calm things.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then it could be a perfect fit. Many community centers run gentle classes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The running shop wants to do a gait analysis before selling me shoes. Is that worth it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It can help, especially if you've had injuries. They watch how your foot lands and suggest shoes that suit you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Or is it just a way to sell expensive shoes?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sometimes it's a bit of both. Comfort is the most important thing, research says choosing what feels best works well.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So I should just try them on?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, try several pairs and jog around in them if the shop lets you. Go in the afternoon, when your feet are a little bigger.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Bigger in the afternoon? / That's weird.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Feet swell a bit during the day, and even more when you run. Leave about a thumb's width at the toe.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It's dark at five, it's raining, and I haven't worked out in three weeks. I just can't be bothered.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Winter slumps hit almost everyone. Be kind to yourself, three weeks is not a disaster.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Feels like one.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: I get that. The trick is to make the next workout tiny, like ten minutes, so it's easy to start.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ten minutes won't do anything.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It does more than zero, and starting is the hard part. Often you'll keep going once you're moving.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Maybe. I could / do something at home I guess.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good idea. A short video workout in your living room, no rain involved. Put your trainers by the sofa now.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My friend says knees should never go past your toes when you squat. True?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's an old rule that isn't really true for most people. Knees going forward is natural, especially if you're tall.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So I can just let them go?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, as long as your heels stay down and your knees track over your toes, not collapsing inward.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How deep should I go?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: As deep as you can while keeping your back neutral and heels down. For many people that's thighs parallel or lower.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My heels lift / when I go low.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That often means tight ankles. Try putting small plates under your heels and work on ankle mobility.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I can swim, but I can't breathe properly doing front crawl. I end up gasping after one length.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's usually because people hold their breath underwater. Breathe out slowly through your nose or mouth while your face is in the water.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Breathe out underwater?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, then when you turn your head, your lungs are ready to take a quick breath in.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: When do I turn my head?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Every two or three strokes. Rotate your body and keep one eye in the water, don't lift your whole head.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: This is a lot to think about / all at once.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Practice the breathing standing in the shallow end first. Bubbles out, turn, breathe in, repeat.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Bubbles, turn, breathe. Got it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You'll get it. Most people need a few sessions.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is jumping rope actually good cardio, or is it just for boxers in movies?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's genuinely great cardio. Ten minutes of skipping is a tough workout, and it improves coordination too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I tried yesterday and kept tripping.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Everybody does at first. Make sure the rope length is right, the handles should reach your armpits when you stand on the middle.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mine's definitely too long.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That makes it much harder. Shorten it with a knot, and keep your jumps small, just off the ground.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long should I do it / as a beginner?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try thirty seconds on, thirty seconds rest, for ten rounds. Do it on a soft surface to protect your joints.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I have asthma. Can I still get into running?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Many people with asthma run, including top athletes. It's worth talking to your doctor about a plan first.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What kind of plan?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Often using your inhaler before exercise, and having it with you on every run.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Cold air seems to set me off.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's common. A scarf or buff over your mouth warms the air. Warm up gradually rather than starting fast.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I avoid / certain times or places?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Avoid busy roads with traffic fumes, and high pollen days if pollen is a trigger. Parks in the morning are often good.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, I'll book a doctor's appointment first.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Great idea. Then start gently and build up.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long should I rest between sets? I usually scroll my phone until I feel like it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a very common approach. It depends on your goal, though.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Strength, mostly. Getting stronger.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: For heavy strength work, two to three minutes is good. That lets your muscles recover enough to lift heavy again.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And for, like, arm stuff?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: For smaller muscles or lighter weights, sixty to ninety seconds is usually enough.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So the scrolling / is fine as long as I time it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. Set a timer on your phone so ten minutes of videos don't sneak in.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My daughter is fourteen and starting pre-season for football. How can she get fitter without overdoing it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good that you're thinking about it. A mix of running, some short sprints and basic strength work is ideal.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Strength work at fourteen?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Bodyweight exercises like squats, lunges and planks are safe and help prevent injuries.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How many days a week?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Three or four sessions, with rest days in between. Keep the sprints short and the jogging easy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She tends to / go all out every time.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then remind her that rest is part of training. Sleep and good food matter just as much at her age.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She'll roll her eyes at me.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Maybe let her coach say it then. It often lands better.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it a good idea to work out with a hangover? Asking for, um, me.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ha. Light exercise can make you feel better, but a hard workout is not a great plan.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What counts as light?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A gentle walk or some easy stretching. Skip heavy lifting and high intensity stuff today.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I was going to do a spin class.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Probably not the day for it. You're likely dehydrated, and intense sweating makes that worse.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Water and a walk then. Maybe / some toast first.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good plan. Drink plenty of water and maybe something with salt in it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've been training for two months and the scale hasn't moved. I'm so frustrated.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's understandable. But the scale is only one measure, and if you're lifting, you might be building muscle as you lose fat.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How would I even know?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Measure your waist, take a photo every few weeks in the same light, and notice how your clothes fit.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My jeans are a bit looser, actually.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a great sign. Strength counts too. Are you lifting more than you did in week one?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Way more. My squat / went up by twenty kilos.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's real progress. Keep going, and weigh yourself less often, maybe once a week at the same time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. That makes me feel better.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It should. You're doing well.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Are ice baths actually good after a workout, or just a social media thing?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: There's some evidence they reduce soreness, but they may also slightly blunt muscle growth if you use them right after lifting.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Huh. So not for gym days?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Probably better after tough endurance sessions or between games, when recovery matters more than building muscle.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about a cold shower instead?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A cold shower is a gentler version. Some people find it refreshing, but benefits are smaller.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My gym has / one of those cold plunge tubs.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then try it after a hard run sometime. Start with a minute or two, and get out if you feel unwell.

option_sets.lead_in: I want to start exercising again and I'm stuck between a few options.
options: The first one is joining the gym near my office, it's pricey but I'd go right after work.
Then there's running outside, totally free, but I tend to skip it when the weather's bad.
And the last one is a home workout app with short twenty minute sessions I can do in the living room.
moshi_comment: The gym near your office has a big advantage, going right after work makes it easy to build a habit. Running is free, but if bad weather stops you, it might not stick. The home app is the most flexible, and twenty minutes is easy to fit in.

What's stopped you in the past, time, money, or motivation? If it's motivation, the gym after work is probably best because it becomes part of your routine. If it's time, the home app is hard to beat.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm training for my first five kilometer race and I'm trying to pick a plan.
options: One plan has me running three days a week, slowly building up over about eight weeks.
Another one mixes running with cycling and swimming, so it's less hard on my knees.
Option three is a run walk method, where I alternate jogging and walking until I can run the whole thing.
And the last is just running every day as far as I can and hoping for the best.
moshi_comment: For a first race, the three days a week plan is a classic for a reason, it gives your body time to recover. The run walk method is great if you're starting from zero. I'd skip running every day, that's a fast way to get hurt.

How much running are you doing right now? If almost none, start with the run walk method. If you can already jog for a bit, the eight week plan is perfect, and the cycling mix is nice if your knees complain.

option_sets.lead_in: I want to sign up for one event this autumn to keep me motivated, and I've found a few.
options: A half marathon in the city, flat and fast, with thousands of people cheering along the route.
A muddy trail race in the forest, about fifteen kilometers, with some steep climbs and river crossings.
An obstacle course with walls, ropes and a lot of mud, and you can enter as a team with friends.
moshi_comment: If you want structure, the half marathon gives you a clear training plan and a great atmosphere. The trail race is tougher but beautiful. The obstacle course is the most fun, especially with friends, though it's less about running.

It depends what keeps you going. Friends and laughs point to the obstacle course, while a big goal points to the half marathon. The trail race sits in between and is a nice change if you're tired of pavements.

option_sets.lead_in: My gym has a new timetable and I can fit in one class a week. Help me pick.
options: There's spin on Monday evenings, very intense, with loud music and an instructor who shouts a lot.
A weights class on Wednesdays where everyone uses barbells, good for strength but it gets crowded.
Yoga on Friday lunchtimes, slow and calm, which my tight hamstrings would probably thank me for.
Or the Sunday morning swim group, which mixes drills and laps, but means getting up early on the weekend.
moshi_comment: If you already do cardio on your own, the weights class or yoga would add the most. Yoga could really help those hamstrings. Spin is great fun if you love the energy, and the swim group is good but Sunday mornings can be hard to keep.

I'd think about what you skip on your own. Most people don't stretch, so yoga fills a gap. The weights class would build strength, though crowds can be annoying. Spin and swimming are both solid cardio choices.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm finally starting a proper strength program and there are so many styles to choose from.
options: Full body workouts three times a week, hitting every muscle each time with a few big lifts.
A push, pull and legs split, which means going five or six days a week to do it properly.
Bodyweight training at home, like push-ups, pull-ups and lunges, with no equipment at all.
moshi_comment: For a beginner, the full body routine is hard to beat, three sessions is manageable and you practice the main lifts often. The split works better once you're more experienced and have more time. Bodyweight training is great if the gym is the obstacle.

How many days can you realistically train? If it's three, go full body. If you love the idea of training most days, the split could work. Bodyweight is a solid start too, and you can always add weights later.

option_sets.lead_in: My rest days are a mess. I've got some ideas for what to do on them.
options: Total rest, sofa, films, nothing at all, which feels great but makes me stiff the next day.
A long easy walk with the dog, maybe an hour, just to keep moving.
A stretching and foam rolling session, about thirty minutes, which I always say I'll do and never do.
Or a gentle swim, which loosens everything up but means going to the pool and back.
moshi_comment: The dog walk is a great default, it's easy, you'll do it anyway, and it helps you recover. Add ten minutes of stretching after it and you've covered two of your ideas. Save the full sofa days for when you're really tired.

Active recovery usually beats doing nothing, so the walk or the swim are good bets. Stretching is useful but only if you'll actually do it, so keep it short. Total rest is fine now and then, just not every time.
